title: Muscle Relaxers and Alcohol: Risks and How Long to Wait
excerpt: Can you drink on muscle relaxers? Why Flexeril, Robaxin, Zanaflex, Soma, and baclofen clash with alcohol, how long to wait between a pill and a drink, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on muscle relaxers? Why Flexeril, Zanaflex, Soma, and baclofen clash with alcohol, how long to wait, and warning signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink while you're taking a prescription muscle relaxer. Nearly every drug in this group works by calming down the brain and spinal cord, and alcohol is a brain depressant too. Put them together and the effects stack: you get far sleepier, dizzier, and clumsier than either would make you alone, and at higher amounts your breathing can slow to a dangerous level. Even one drink with one pill can leave you far more impaired than you expect, and the combination is a common cause of falls, car crashes, and emergency visits, and the labels for these medicines warn against it. This guide explains why the two clash, how the most common muscle relaxers compare, how long to wait between a pill and a drink, and the warning signs that mean you should get help now.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on days you take a muscle relaxer. Don't take a muscle relaxer after drinking, for a hangover, or to help you sleep after a night out. Never drive after combining them. Be extra careful if you also take opioid painkillers, sleep aids, anxiety medicines like Xanax or Valium, gabapentin, or sedating antihistamines. If someone has combined muscle relaxers and alcohol and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has blue or gray lips, **call 911 right away.**

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist.** This article explains how muscle relaxers and alcohol interact and what official labeling says. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and it does not give dosing advice. **Talk to your prescriber** before drinking at all while on a muscle relaxer, if you've already been mixing them, or if you want to stop or change your medicine. Some muscle relaxers, especially baclofen, can cause serious withdrawal if stopped suddenly, so don't quit one on your own to make room for drinking. If you're in the US and worried about a possible overdose, Poison Control is available 24/7 at **1-800-222-1222**. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why Muscle Relaxers and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Mechanism in Plain Words

"Muscle relaxer" sounds like a drug that works directly on your muscles. Most don't. The common prescription muscle relaxers, such as cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril; see our [cyclobenzaprine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/cyclobenzaprine-and-alcohol)), methocarbamol (Robaxin), tizanidine (Zanaflex), carisoprodol (Soma), and metaxalone (Skelaxin), act mainly on the **central nervous system**, which is your brain and spinal cord. They turn down the nerve signals that keep a muscle tense or in spasm. That's why the most common side effect on all of their labels is the same one: drowsiness.

Alcohol is also a central nervous system depressant. It boosts the brain's main "slow down" signal (a chemical messenger called GABA) and blocks one of its main "speed up" signals (glutamate). That's what makes you relaxed, then sleepy, then uncoordinated as you drink more.

When you combine two drugs that both slow the nervous system, the effects don't just sit side by side. They add together, and sometimes one makes the other stronger than you'd predict. Doctors call this an **additive** or **synergistic** effect. In practice it shows up as:

- **Heavy drowsiness** that comes on faster and lasts longer than usual.
- **Dizziness and poor balance,** which is why falls are such a common problem, especially in older adults.
- **Slowed reaction time and poor judgment,** which makes driving dangerous even when you feel "fine."
- **Memory gaps,** where you don't remember parts of the evening.
- **Slowed or shallow breathing** at higher amounts, especially when a third sedating drug such as an opioid is involved. This is the part that can be fatal.

### Some muscle relaxers have a second problem

A few muscle relaxers bring extra risks on top of the shared sedation:

- **Tizanidine (Zanaflex)** can drop your blood pressure, and alcohol can too, so the pair can make you lightheaded or faint when you stand up. The Zanaflex label also notes that alcohol increases the amount of tizanidine in your blood.
- **Carisoprodol (Soma)** is broken down in the body into meprobamate, an older anti-anxiety drug. It's a controlled substance in the US because of its potential for misuse, and combining it with alcohol or opioids is especially risky.
- **Baclofen** acts directly on GABA receptors, the same system alcohol targets, so the overlap is especially close.
- **Diazepam (Valium)** is a benzodiazepine that's sometimes prescribed for muscle spasms. Benzodiazepines carry an FDA boxed warning (the strongest kind) about slowed breathing when combined with opioids, and their labels also warn against alcohol for the same reason.
- **Chlorzoxazone and dantrolene** have both been linked to rare liver injury, so adding regular heavy drinking puts extra load on an organ that's already doing work.

## How the Common Muscle Relaxers Compare

Here is a plain-language overview of the muscle relaxers people most often ask about. "Half-life" means the time it takes your body to clear half of a dose. A longer half-life means the drug sticks around longer, so the window where alcohol is a problem is longer too. Half-lives vary between people, and older adults and people with liver or kidney problems usually clear these drugs more slowly.

| Drug (brand) | How it's usually used | Approximate half-life | Extra concern with alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril, Amrix) | Short-term back and neck spasms | Long, often around 18 hours, and longer in older adults | Very sedating; related to tricyclic antidepressants |
| Methocarbamol (Robaxin) | Short-term muscle spasms | Short, about 1 to 2 hours | Drowsiness and dizziness |
| Tizanidine (Zanaflex) | Spasticity (from MS, spinal injury) and sometimes spasms | Short, about 2 to 3 hours | Low blood pressure, fainting; alcohol raises drug levels |
| Baclofen (Lioresal, others) | Spasticity | About 2 to 6 hours | Acts on GABA like alcohol; dangerous to stop suddenly |
| Carisoprodol (Soma) | Short-term muscle pain | About 2 hours, but its active by-product lasts much longer | Controlled substance; misuse and breathing risk |
| Metaxalone (Skelaxin) | Short-term muscle pain | Roughly 9 hours | Drowsiness, dizziness |
| Orphenadrine (Norflex) | Short-term muscle pain | Long, often more than 12 hours | Drowsiness, dry mouth, confusion |
| Diazepam (Valium) | Spasms, anxiety | Very long; it and its by-products can last days | Benzodiazepine; serious breathing risk |

The takeaway from this table isn't that some of these are fine with alcohol. None of them is. It's that the safe gap between a dose and a drink is very different depending on which one you take, which is the next question people usually ask.

## How Long After Taking a Muscle Relaxer Can You Drink?

This is the most searched question on the topic, and there's no single number that fits everyone. Your prescription label will usually just say to avoid alcohol. If you want a more specific answer, here's how pharmacists tend to think about it.

**The five half-life rule of thumb.** After about five half-lives, almost all of a single dose has left your body. That gives rough timelines like these for a **single dose** in a healthy adult:

- **Short-acting drugs** (methocarbamol, tizanidine, chlorzoxazone): roughly 10 to 15 hours.
- **Middle-range drugs** (baclofen, metaxalone): roughly a day to two days.
- **Long-acting drugs** (cyclobenzaprine, orphenadrine): several days.
- **Diazepam (Valium):** a week or more for the drug and its by-products to fully clear, although the strongest sedation wears off sooner.

These are rough guides, not permission. Three things change the picture:

1. **If you take it on a schedule, you're never "between" doses.** Someone taking cyclobenzaprine three times a day for a back injury has a steady level in their blood the whole time. There's no safe evening to drink until the course is finished and the drug has cleared.
2. **Age, liver, and kidneys matter.** Older adults and people with liver or kidney disease clear many of these drugs more slowly, so the window is longer.
3. **Other medicines stack too.** If you're also taking an opioid, a sleep aid, an anxiety medicine, or gabapentin, the combined effect is larger and lasts longer.

The simplest safe plan: if you're on a short course of a muscle relaxer, skip alcohol until the course is done and a few days have passed. If you have an event coming up, ask your prescriber or pharmacist for a timing plan in advance. They can look at your exact drug, dose, and other medicines.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take a Muscle Relaxer?

The other direction matters too. If you drank last night and wake up with a sore back, it's tempting to reach for a muscle relaxer. Wait.

- **Let the alcohol clear first.** The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies widely. After six or eight drinks, alcohol can still be in your system the next morning, even if you've slept. If someone seems far more out of it than a normal hangover, our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers the red flags.
- **Wait until you feel completely sober,** not just "less drunk."
- **Don't use a muscle relaxer as a sleep aid after drinking.** That's the exact situation where breathing can slow overnight with nobody watching.

If you're stiff and sore after a night out, ordinary hangover aches usually come from dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, and whatever you did on the dance floor. Our guide to [body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking) explains what helps and when aches are a sign of something more serious.

## Can You Take a Muscle Relaxer for a Hangover?

No. Muscle relaxers don't treat any cause of a hangover. They don't fix dehydration, low blood sugar, poor sleep, or the inflammation that alcohol triggers. What they do is add sedation on top of whatever alcohol is still in your system, which is the opposite of what you want when you're trying to function the next day.

If your hangover comes with a headache or body aches, a standard dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever with food is usually the more sensible option, though those have their own alcohol cautions. Ibuprofen and naproxen are harder on the stomach after drinking (see our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol)), and acetaminophen adds work for the liver (see [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol)). Water, food, rest, and time remain the basics.

## The Dangerous Combinations: Muscle Relaxers, Alcohol, and Other Sedatives

The serious emergencies usually don't involve just a muscle relaxer and a couple of beers. They involve three or more sedating substances at once. A back injury is a common example: someone may be prescribed a muscle relaxer **and** an opioid painkiller, then have a few drinks to unwind. Each one slows breathing a little. Together they can slow it a lot, often during sleep.

Be especially careful if you take any of these alongside a muscle relaxer:

- **Opioid painkillers** such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, tramadol, or codeine.
- **Benzodiazepines** such as alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), clonazepam (Klonopin), or diazepam (Valium). See our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol).
- **Gabapentin or pregabalin (Lyrica),** which are often prescribed for nerve pain alongside muscle relaxers. See [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).
- **Sleep medicines** such as zolpidem (Ambien), and over-the-counter sleep aids containing diphenhydramine or doxylamine, including many "PM" products.
- **Some antidepressants,** especially sedating ones. Cyclobenzaprine in particular can interact with certain antidepressants, including a risk of a reaction called serotonin syndrome with some of them.

Carisoprodol (Soma) deserves a specific mention. Combining it with opioids and benzodiazepines has been linked in the medical literature to misuse and overdose deaths, which is one reason it's now a controlled substance in the US. If you've been prescribed Soma, alcohol is a firm no.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

> **Call 911 right away if someone who has combined a muscle relaxer with alcohol (or other sedatives):**
> - Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake and falls back asleep immediately
> - Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or is making loud snoring or gurgling sounds they can't be roused from
> - Has blue or gray lips or fingertips, or cold, clammy skin
> - Is confused, can't speak clearly, or is having a seizure
> - Has vomited while very drowsy
>
> While you wait: don't leave them alone, don't let them "sleep it off," and roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit. If opioids may also be involved and naloxone (Narcan) is available, use it. It won't hurt someone who hasn't taken opioids.

> **Talk to a doctor soon (same day or next day) if you notice:**
> - Fainting or nearly fainting when you stand up, especially on tizanidine
> - A fall or head injury while under the influence, even if you feel okay
> - Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs while taking chlorzoxazone, dantrolene, or tizanidine
> - Agitation, fever, sweating, muscle twitching, or a racing heart if you take cyclobenzaprine with an antidepressant
> - Hallucinations, seizures, or severe agitation after missing doses of baclofen

For a broader checklist of what too much alcohol looks like, see our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs).

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people have a much smaller margin for error with this combination:

- **Adults over 65.** Muscle relaxers are on the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria list of medicines that are often a poor fit for older adults, mainly because of sedation, confusion, and fall risk. Alcohol adds to all three.
- **Anyone also taking opioids, benzodiazepines, gabapentin, or sleep aids.** This is the group where breathing problems happen.
- **People with sleep apnea or lung disease,** whose breathing is already vulnerable during sleep.
- **People with liver or kidney disease,** who clear many of these drugs more slowly.
- **Anyone who will drive,** operate machinery, or care for a child the same day.
- **People taking baclofen long term.** It's dangerous to skip doses or stop suddenly, so don't stop it to make room for a night out. Ask your doctor instead.

If any of these describe you, take five minutes with a pharmacist. They can check your full medication list for interactions you might not know about. For more on how common medicines and supplements interact, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## What About Over-the-Counter Muscle Rubs and "Natural" Muscle Relaxers?

Not everything sold for sore muscles is a central nervous system drug.

- **Topical rubs and patches** (menthol, camphor, lidocaine, or diclofenac gel) work on the skin and the area underneath. They're generally not a sedation concern with alcohol. Diclofenac gel is an anti-inflammatory, though, so if you're already taking ibuprofen or naproxen by mouth, ask a pharmacist before doubling up.
- **Magnesium** is often marketed for muscle cramps. It isn't a sedative in the way prescription muscle relaxers are, but high doses can cause diarrhea, and the evidence for cramps is mixed.
- **Herbal "relaxation" products** like valerian, kava, or high-dose CBD can add to alcohol's sedating effects. Kava in particular has been linked to liver problems. Treat these with the same caution as a prescription sedative.
- **In some countries,** muscle relaxer combinations are sold over the counter (for example, products containing methocarbamol or orphenadrine with a pain reliever). They carry the same alcohol risks as the prescription versions, plus whatever risk comes with the added painkiller.

## A Practical Plan If You've Been Prescribed a Muscle Relaxer

Most prescriptions for muscle relaxers are for short courses, often a week or two for back or neck pain. That makes the practical plan pretty simple:

1. **Ask at the pharmacy counter.** When you pick up the prescription, ask, "How long after my last dose can I have a drink?" Pharmacists answer this question all the time.
2. **Plan around events.** If you have a wedding or a trip during the course, tell your prescriber in advance. Sometimes the timing can be adjusted, or a different approach to the pain can be used.
3. **If you do slip up and have a drink,** don't take your next dose until the alcohol has cleared, don't drive, and have someone around. Watch for the warning signs above.
4. **Store the bottle safely.** Muscle relaxers are commonly misused, and leftovers in a medicine cabinet are a risk to teenagers and visitors. Dispose of unused pills through a pharmacy take-back program.
5. **Don't share or borrow them.** A dose that's fine for one person can be too much for another, especially combined with alcohol.

## Supporting Your Body When You Do Drink

Once you're off the muscle relaxer and it's cleared your system, normal drinking advice applies. Most of what makes the morning after easier is basic: eat before and while you drink, alternate alcohol with water, set a drink limit before you start, and stop a few hours before bed so your sleep isn't wrecked. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the full checklist.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. It's not a sedative and it's not a muscle relaxer, and there is no good evidence that it makes it safe to combine alcohol with any sedating medication. If you're curious, our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people typically use it. As with any supplement, check with your doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Muscle relaxers and alcohol both slow your brain and nervous system, and together they can make you far more drowsy, dizzy, and impaired than you expect. At higher amounts, especially with opioids or other sedatives, they can slow breathing to a dangerous level. The safest approach is to skip alcohol while you're taking a muscle relaxer, wait until the drug has cleared before drinking again (that can be half a day or several days depending on which one you take), and never use a muscle relaxer to treat a hangover or help you sleep after drinking. When in doubt, ask your pharmacist. It's a quick conversation that can prevent a fall, a crash, or something worse.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking muscle relaxers?**

It's best not to. Almost every prescription muscle relaxer slows down the brain and nervous system, and alcohol does the same thing. Together they add up, causing heavy drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, falls, and in larger amounts slowed breathing. The labels for these drugs warn against combining them with alcohol. If you've been prescribed one, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether any drinking is acceptable for your specific drug and dose.

**How long after taking a muscle relaxer can I drink alcohol?**

It depends on the drug, because they leave the body at very different speeds. A common pharmacist rule of thumb is to wait about five half-lives, which works out to roughly 10 hours or more for short-acting drugs like methocarbamol or tizanidine, and several days for cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) or diazepam (Valium). If you take the drug on a schedule, you're never really between doses. Ask your pharmacist for the waiting time that fits your exact prescription.

**How long after drinking can I take a muscle relaxer?**

Wait until the alcohol has fully cleared and you feel completely sober, not just less drunk. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot from person to person. After a heavy night, that can mean waiting well into the next day. Don't take a muscle relaxer for a hangover or to help you sleep after drinking.

**What happens if you mix Flexeril and alcohol?**

Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) is chemically related to older tricyclic antidepressants and is strongly sedating on its own. With alcohol, people often feel very drowsy, dizzy, and uncoordinated, and they may have trouble with memory, balance, and judgment. Larger amounts raise the risk of falls, car crashes, and dangerously slowed breathing, especially if other sedating drugs are involved. Its label warns that it may increase the effects of alcohol.

**Which muscle relaxer is safest with alcohol?**

None of them is considered safe to combine with alcohol. Some are shorter-acting, which means they clear the body faster, but every common prescription muscle relaxer can add to alcohol's sedating effects. Carisoprodol (Soma), diazepam (Valium), and baclofen carry extra concerns. If you know you'll be at an event where you want to drink, tell your prescriber ahead of time so they can plan around it.

**Can one beer with a muscle relaxer hurt you?**

Yes, it can. Even one drink with a single dose can make you far more drowsy and impaired than you expect, and the labels for these medicines don't set any amount of alcohol as safe. That matters if you drive, climb stairs, or care for someone. The risk climbs with more drinks, higher doses, older age, and other sedating medicines like opioids, sleep aids, or anxiety pills. Don't drive after combining them.

**Is it dangerous to take a muscle relaxer for a hangover?**

Yes, it's a bad idea. Muscle relaxers don't treat any cause of a hangover, and if alcohol is still in your system they stack on top of it. For hangover aches, rest, fluids, food, and time are the safer basics. If body aches after drinking are severe or come with weakness or dark urine, see a doctor.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on muscle relaxers?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM protects against the combined sedating effects of alcohol and muscle relaxers, and it should not be used for that purpose. DHM has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animals with limited human data. If you take a muscle relaxer, follow your prescriber's advice about alcohol regardless of any supplement.
